Shameless creative report, three months: what won and lost every month, what customers are telling us, and where it cashes on the way to $115M

Meta, 2026-06-08 to 2026-09-06 (thirteen weeks), every creative with $400+ spend (450 creatives, $1,659,256). Source: ejam-dwh creative_dashboard (brand SHA, channel facebook), goal_vs_actual, ClickUp briefs, winners archive, Facebook ad-comment digests June 16 to September 8. Built 2026-09-08. The four-week version (Aug 10 to Sep 6) is here.
1 The three months2 Winning themes2a Top 25 by spend3 Funnel trends by type4 Other channels5 What customers care about6 Next sprint7 The $115M lens8 Every cited ad, two notes each9 Full population

Thirteen weeks of Meta spend, June 8 to September 6, every creative over $400, read against the winner canon, the landing-page funnel, and the ad-comment digests from June to September. The short version is the same as the four-week report, with the trend behind it: the account sells candy abundance, not fiber, and three months of data say so in every month. What wins is a box full of flavors, a number the viewer can check against candy they already eat, retail proof, and a real order being packed. What lost, all three months, is curiosity copy the click resolves, problem-first health framing, weight-loss testimonials, and creator ads sent straight to a product page.

Contribution = revenue − COGS − spend (before agency and merchant fees), per creative, first-order attribution only. Negative on order one is normal for SHA; subscriptions pay back on rebills. Only 7 creatives with $1,000+ spend clear breakeven on contribution across the three months, none of them over $5k of spend. July alone was $869,863 at 0.86 and -$385,172 of contribution, 53% of the loss.

Mechanisms named in this report: Show the box · Same-number reveal · Countable proof · Get all of them · The launch bump · Pre-living the order · Anchor before the page · The closed loop (why curiosity copy loses) · Cold click (why cheap clicks don't convert) · Money follows age (why the biggest lines are the oldest) · Candy first, catch second.

1. The three months in one table

Spend went from about $64k a week in June to $307k in the week of 07-13, then back to $102k by late August. ROAS did not move with it: 0.81 to 0.90 every week except the launch week of August 31 (0.75, live ads 1175 against 672 the week before). Scaling did not break the account and did not lift it; the July bets (SH-16180-1 ▶ at $132k, SH-16917-1 ▶ at $84k, the weight-loss creator batch at $130k, the flavor launches at $168k) all landed between 0.77 and 0.86.

Two things moved under the flat line. Video and static converged: statics ran 0.94 to 1.06 in June when they were small and cheap, 0.79 to 0.86 at July scale; video ran 0.66 to 0.77 in June while the Trybe cuts carried it, 0.79 to 0.85 in July, then 0.80 to 0.92 in August once the haul, warehouse and Target lines took the money. And LP to add-to-cart rose from 23% in early June to 32% in mid July and has held 26 to 30% since, which is the haul lane on TRW-Gifts replacing creator UGC on Shopify.

What the table says. Two themes were above 1.0 in August: Target proof and the warehouse comment-reply. Two more sit just under it because one big creative drags them: the haul (0.97 in August; the caption cold open runs 1.04, the count-the-bags video 0.91) and the launch statics (0.98; the ones that look like the page run 1.2 to 1.6, the scaled launch bag 0.78). Four themes lost in every month they ran: weight-loss creator testimonials ($201,002 at 0.76, falling 0.79, 0.69, 0.57 month by month), creator UGC sent to Shopify ($161,665 at 0.67), the Amazon riddle ($72,653 at 0.63) and fiber-first ($140,731 at 0.81). Those four are $576,051 of spend and -$305,620 of contribution, 42% of the three-month loss on 35% of the spend.

The launch bump. The variety-pack theme ran 1.42 in June on $22k, 0.95 in July on $168k. Every flavor drop converts at 1.2 to 1.6 for its first $1k to $2k (SH-16132-11 ▣ 1.61, SH-16143-3 ▣ 1.64, SH-16157-4 ▣ 1.56, SH-16478-7 ▶ 1.63, SH-16616-5 ▶ 1.56) and then either gets capped there or gets scaled into a static that no longer says anything new (SH-16158 ▣ 0.78 on $33k in July). The pattern for Mini Bites on September 15 is the top three launch statics with a real budget, not 140 statics at $1.9k each.

Mechanism: Countable proof

Retail proof: sold out at Target

2 ads · $143,828 · ROAS 1.04 · contribution -$46,679 · LP→ATC 32.8% · Jun $16k @ 1.07 · July $75k @ 1.02 · August $46k @ 1.04 · Sep $7k @ 1.15
SH-13376-6SH-13376-9

SH-13376-6 ▣ SPOTTED AT TARGET: THE SNACK EVERYONE'S GRABBING FIRST and SH-13376-9 ▣ NOW AT TARGET. GONE BEFORE YOU GET THERE took $143,828 over three months at 1.04, above 1.0 in June, July, August and September. It is the only theme over $100k that pays, and it is two creatives. No faces, a banner sandwich over a pile of bags, a claim you can verify in a store, routed to the Target page whose ATC to order is the best in the account.

The Customer Testimonial angle tag (which is this family) is the second-best static angle of the window at 1.03 on $82,356. Two variations in thirteen weeks is the most under-iterated proven static in the account, and the Amazon "record-breaking" claim, which lost $43k on the riddle layout, belongs on this layout.

Mechanism: Pre-living the order

Pack it for Sarah: comment-reply order packing

11 ads · $64,020 · ROAS 1.05 · contribution -$20,298 · LP→ATC 38.2% · Jun $4k @ 0.77 · July $32k @ 1.07 · August $24k @ 1.09 · Sep $4k @ 0.88
SH-15191-5SH-12937-7SH-11965-1SH-16212-10

$64,020 at 1.05 and 38.2% LP to ATC, the best conversion of any theme, 1.07 in July and 1.09 in August. The format is a reply to a named customer's comment ("All right, Sarah, love your choices") followed by her order being packed on camera. The viewer watches their own order happen before they place it. SH-15191-5 ▶ carried $41k at 47% ATC; SH-12937-7 ▶ (a quiz that answers itself) 1.70 and contribution positive; SH-11965-1 ▶ 1.21 at 85 seconds.

The exception proves the routing rule: SH-8654-7 ▶, the same format sent straight to the Shopify product page, ran 0.78. No creator fee, no script, and the newest cut in the family is from July.

Mechanism: Show the box

The haul: show the box, not the bag

13 ads · $300,057 · ROAS 0.91 · contribution -$123,910 · LP→ATC 39.1% · Jun $26k @ 1.03 · July $163k @ 0.86 · August $96k @ 0.97 · Sep $15k @ 1.02
SH-16975-2SH-16180-1SH-17155-4SH-16469

The biggest theme in the account ($300,057, 18% of spend) and the best converter at scale (39.1% LP to ATC). A shipper box of 12 bags being opened, spilled, or pulled from. SH-16975-2 ▶ opens on a burned-in caption, HOW IS THIS EVEN LEGAL?: $63k at 1.05 with no fatigue across three months. SH-16180-1 ▶ counts the bags out loud: $200k, 38% ATC every month, and ROAS that tracks budget (1.00 at $15k in June, 0.82 at $132k in July, 1.01 at $8k in September). SH-17155-4 ▶ and SH-16469 ▶ do it hands-only.

The hook is a mechanic, not a line. The caption cold open beat every spoken opener in the family and held its return at scale; the spoken count did not. Quantity on screen is value felt before price is said. The lane's problem is concentration: two creators, one box, and the biggest one has been allowed to run at 0.82 for $132k in a month.

Mechanism: Get all of them, and the launch bump

Variety as acquisition: the launch statics that look like the page

141 ads · $268,519 · ROAS 0.99 · contribution -$95,837 · LP→ATC 33.3% · Jun $22k @ 1.42 · July $168k @ 0.95 · August $68k @ 0.98 · Sep $10k @ 0.85
SH-16132-11SH-16143-3SH-16535-9SH-16313-2SH-16478-7SH-16616-5

141 creatives, $268,519, 0.99: Berry Blast, All-Stars, Sweet and Sour, Tropical Paradise, Super Sour and the four-pack, June to August. The best statics of the whole window live here and they all say the same three things: the bag, the numbers, "new": SH-16132-11 ▣ 26g of fiber. 3g of sugar. Five sour berry flavors 1.61, SH-16143-3 ▣ 5 REASONS TO GRAB THE BERRY BLAST DROP 1.64, SH-16535-9 ▣ FOUR NEW FLAVORS YOU WON'T FIND ON A SHELF 1.41, SH-16313-2 ▣ the six-bag menu 1.30 at 40% ATC. On video, SH-16478-7 ▶ (an eight-second bag spin, PARADISE, MINUS THE SUGAR) 1.63 and SH-16616-5 ▶ 1.56.

The choice version loses (SH-16464-8 ▣ BERRY LOVER, OR TROPICAL SOUL? behind "get all of them"), the abstract comparison loses (SH-16152 ▣ Same craving. Not the same candy 0.50), and the launch static that got scaled after the bump (SH-16158 ▣, 0.78 on $33k in July) loses. Launch energy is worth 1.2 to 1.6 for two weeks; after that only the menu and the numbers hold.

Mechanism: Same-number reveal

The same-number reveal: 70 calories against candy they know

24 ads · $117,868 · ROAS 0.84 · contribution -$54,056 · LP→ATC 34.5% · Jun $5k @ 1.07 · July $96k @ 0.81 · August $12k @ 1.06 · Sep $5k @ 0.74
SH-16975-3SH-16192SH-16917-1SH-16140-4

Bimodal. SH-16975-3 ▶ "This one bag is 880 calories", holding a full-sugar bag then ours, is the best creative in three months: 1.96 ROAS, +$746 contribution at a $33 CPA, and it was allowed $2.9k. SH-16192 ▶, the QVC retro, lands the same beat spoken ("each bag is 70 calories") with a $2.69 badge on screen, 1.43. SH-16140-4 ▣ Berry Blast vs. a bowl of berries 1.27 on a static. Then the July bet: SH-16917-1 ▶, the paddle edit that runs the pairs (70 vs 70, then 3g vs 23g of sugar) and adds a "cheap garbage" verdict and a sale close, $84k at 0.80 and minus $41k. The pairs bought the cart (37% ATC); the verdict and the close lost the sale.

What makes it work is parity first. Seventy against seventy neutralises calories before anything diverges, so the sugar and fiber beats read as pure gain. Candy first, the catch second, one concrete comparator, no verdict. Fiber-first opens lost on the same footage all window (the SH-17215 same-creator pair: candy opener 0.92, fiber opener 0.68).

Mechanism: Anchor before the page

Price and deadline before the click

18 ads · $71,970 · ROAS 1.09 · contribution -$21,231 · LP→ATC 38.6% · Jun $17k @ 1.27 · July $21k @ 1.31 · August $29k @ 0.86 · Sep $5k @ 0.86
SH-13107-6SH-13396-1SH-16521-10SH-14498-8

$71,970 at 1.09, 38.6% ATC. The offer lane ran 1.27 in June and 1.31 in July on real deadlines (SH-13107-6 ▣ THE SALE IS ENDING 1.40 on $24k, SH-13396-1 ▶ the "final bow" letter 1.37 with the highest ATC of the window, 57%) and 0.86 in August when the deadline was replaced by a gift pile (SH-14498-8 ▣ ALL OF THIS FOR FREE, 0.89 on $18k). SH-16521-10 ▣ GET UP TO 46% OFF + FREE GIFTS 1.36. Ads that state the price or the deadline land visitors who already accepted it. It is a wrapper, not a concept: it works on top of candy, not instead of it, and the "46% off is a scam, do the math" comment has followed the offer since June.

What lost, three months running

Weight-loss creator testimonials. 104 videos, $201,002, 0.76 ROAS, -$103,839, 22.2% ATC, mostly on the swap page: 0.79 in July, 0.69 in August, 0.57 in September. The doctor cuts (SH-16360-8 ▶ "it gives you butyrates", $34k at 0.77; SH-16360-1 ▶ "regular and not bloated" 0.81) buy the cheapest clicks in the account and the coldest visitors. The one cut above 1.2, SH-16302-8 ▶, opens "if you love a sour candy" and then says the numbers. Explicit weight framing and talking heads lose to the swap arithmetic on the same page.
Creator UGC sent straight to Shopify. The Trybe bucket, $161,665 at 0.67, -$91,726, $104 CPA, 21.0% ATC, no SH codes, no landing page, no owner. About 25 creators at $2k to $21k each; two above 1.0 (Jeremy Morrison 1.62, LaJuan Carter 1.05). It was $89k in June and $20k in August, so the cut is happening by attrition rather than by decision.
Curiosity and negation copy. The Amazon riddle (SH-15957-7 ▣ July on the swap page, SH-17273-9 ▣ August on the flavor page): $72,653 at 0.63, 18.0% ATC, -$43,463. The wedges (SH-17250-10 ▣ "we can't say", SH-17259-7 ▣ "our lawyers", SH-16152 ▣ "same craving") $33,079 at 0.78 and 15.5% ATC, the worst conversion of any theme. The Curiosity-Driven Hook angle took $116,029 across 15 statics at 0.75, the second most funded angle per ad. The click closes the loop the ad opened and the page starts from zero.
Fiber and gut health first. 47 creatives, $140,731 at 0.81, -$66,593. SH-9428 ▣ 3 cups of broccoli ran all three months at 0.77 to 0.91 with no task and no LP; SH-3028 ▣ Good For Your Gut Health slid 1.10, 0.94, 0.67; the poop statics (SH-14765-7 ▣) 0.70. The Problem-Solution angle ran 0.65, 0.65, 0.55 by month. The fiber era is over on the data in every month of the window.
High-hook talking heads. SH-17338-1 ▶ (59% hook, the highest in the window, 0.76), SH-17207-4 ▶ (38% hook, 0.57, $112 CPA), the QVC edits (SH-15238-1 ▶ 0.74, SH-15688-6 ▶ 0.43). Hook rate against ROAS across the 84 videos over $1,000: Spearman -0.21. Videos under 15% hook returned 1.07; 35% and over returned 0.80.

4. What this means for LPs, site, email and SMS

Ten transfers from paid creative to owned channels, each backed by three months of numbers above or a comment pattern below.

  1. Show the box, not the bag. The shipper box with 12 bags spilling out converts 38 to 46% LP to ATC on $260k over three months. LP hero, PDP first image, email header, SMS MMS: the open box with every flavor visible. Not one bag on a plinth.
  2. Lead with 70 calories against a number they already know. "This one bag is 880 calories." "Berry Blast vs. a bowl of berries." Put a same-number comparison row above the fold on every page and in the first screen of every email: 70 cal vs 70 cal of the candy you buy now, then 3g vs 23g sugar. One concrete comparator, no verdict: the paddle edit that added "cheap garbage" lost $41k.
  3. State the price or the deadline before they scroll. $2.69 a bag, 46% off plus free gifts, "last 2 pallets": in the ad, at the top of the page, in the subject line. The offer lane ran 1.27 to 1.31 with a real deadline and 0.86 with a gift pile. Email and SMS say the per-bag price, not "fiber-packed gummies".
  4. Don't tease on our own pages and emails. "Flips candy logic on its head" and "we can't say..." only work in an ad because the click answers the riddle. On the LP, in an email or an SMS nobody clicks to find out, they leave. First line says the number, the price and the sweetener.
  5. Answer the five questions people ask every week, on-page and pre-click. Sweetener by name and why (the erythritol-and-studies thread has run since the June 16 digest), total vs net carbs with the subtraction shown ("the carb count is like 35g"), pieces per bag, which flavors are not sour, one-time purchase available. A label-math block on the LP, a FAQ footer in email, one line in SMS.
  6. Subscription clarity above the fold. "They automatically charge you even before you say yes" appears in June and again in September on different ads. The overlay "No subscription required. One-time orders available at checkout." ran the cheapest CPA in its family. Put that sentence on the offer block, the cart, the welcome email and a pinned comment on every live ad.
  7. Retail proof travels. Target proof is the only theme over $100k above 1.0, and it held for three months. "Are these in stores?" is asked ten times a week. Site header, welcome email, PDP: Target, Amazon rank, review count. Countable proof, not adjectives.
  8. Menu beats hero. The six-bag menu static converts 40%; the "pick one" versions convert the same and close at half the rate. The collection page and every email grid carry the badge system (Best Seller, Fan Favorite, Cult Classic, Sour Pick) and one line per flavor.
  9. Real orders being packed. The warehouse pack-an-order videos hold the top ATC rates in every month they ran. Post-purchase email: "your box is being packed" with a ten-second clip. Site: an orders-packed-today strip. Comments: reply to real people with real packing.
  10. The voice. The TRW-Gifts listicle is the tone standard because it is funny and physical ("feels like eating a yoga mat"). The doctor explaining butyrates on the swap page is the opposite and lost $17k. Every reason carries a bit, the joke targets the category, Shameless is the straight man.

5. What the customer cares about

From what converts in creative over three months, cross-checked against the weekly Facebook ad-comment digests from June 16 to September 8 and the Amazon and DTC review corpus. The striking thing is how little changed: the June 16 digest's top six themes (erythritol studies, flavor requests, price per piece, GI effects, sweetener transparency, subscription friction) are the September 8 digest's top six.

  1. It has to be real candy first. Taste surprise is the number-one unprompted review theme ("makes no sense they taste as good as they do"). Every winning ad shows candy eaten or piled up; the winning hook cycle is candy, then the catch. Fiber-first opens lost on the same footage in every month, and the one weight-loss creator cut above 1.2 opens "if you love a sour candy".
  2. How much am I getting for the money. Hauls win because the box is the value. The top price objection is per-piece math: "only 15 or 16 candies per bag", "$7 for 5.5 oz", and in June "the 46% off is a scam, $2.69 x 40 is $107.60". The counter-math a customer wrote for us: "A candy bar is nearly $3 for one and these cost less than that per bag and have fiber and WAY less sugar." That is the price frame, and the creator who said "$8 on one pack when you can get 12" ran 1.10.
  3. Calories and sugar they can check. They read the label. "37 grams of carbs!" and "the carb count is like 35g" run from June to September, which means the number they see has to be the number we lead with, and the net-carb subtraction has to be visible. The parity device (70 vs 70) is how the product survives that scrutiny; the paddle edit proved the pairs buy the cart.
  4. What is actually in it. Sweetener anxiety (erythritol, sucralose) was the number-one theme in the June 16 digest, with commenters pasting cardiovascular studies, and it is still roughly 40 comments a week in September, now shifting from taste to safety. No live creative in three months addressed it. Silence reads as hiding; naming the sweetener, the amount and the reason is the only move.
  5. Permission, not a diet. "I allow myself one bag a day", "on a weight loss journey and these are a real treat". The buyer is dieting and wants candy back. Explicit weight framing lost for three months ($201,002 at 0.76, and Meta policy); "keep candy in your life" wins.
  6. Control over the purchase. No subscription trap, order once, know where the package is. "They automatically charge you before you say yes" (June, SH-15951) and the auto-enroll paragraph pasted across three ads (September) are the same complaint. Trust is a conversion variable: the scam accusations sit on the two biggest videos and go unanswered.
  7. Range and discovery. "Which ones aren't sour", black-licorice requests, chili mango restock, "what are these new Shameless flavors everyone's posting". They want to browse, which is why the menu static and "get all four" beat "pick one", and why every flavor drop converts at 1.2 to 1.6 for its first two weeks.
  8. They share the regularity joke, they buy the candy. "Can't poop? Eat this candy" is the top TikTok Shop earner and poop-first statics lost on Meta in every month (0.55 to 0.65 Problem-Solution). Bathroom humor is a creator and comment lever, not a paid-static lever.

6. What to do with this next sprint

  1. Stop funding the two lanes that lost three months running. Weight-loss creator testimonials on the swap page and creator UGC sent to the Shopify product page: $362,667 at 0.72, -$195,564, 22% of the spend and 27% of the loss. Keep the two Trybe creators above 1.0 and the one candy-first WL cut, route them to TRW-Gifts, pause the rest. Give the Trybe bucket an owner.
  2. Fund the haul and parity lane, and cap the count-the-bags video. Five more cuts on the SH-16975 creator pattern: box open, caption cold open, "this one bag is X" against a sourced comparator, one number, no verdict, no sale close. Route to TRW-Gifts. Hold SH-16180-1 ▶ under $10k a week (it runs 1.0 there and 0.82 at $30k) and move the difference into SH-16975-3 ▶ and SH-16975-2 ▶.
  3. Retro the Target proof. Ten headlines on the bag-pile banner sandwich, retail-proof lines only, the Amazon record-breaking line first (the claim lost $43k on the riddle layout, not on its own). Two variations in thirteen weeks is not a family.
  4. Move statics off the flavor-novelty page unless they look like the page, and give the launch effect a budget. Retire the riddles and wedges (SH-17273-9 first). Keep the menu, four-pack and three-number launch layouts. For Mini Bites on September 15: the box hero, the 70 vs 70 row and three launch statics with real money behind them for the two-week bump, not 140 statics at $1.9k.
  5. Ship the label-math creative and the sweetener line. One static and one 15-second cut: 37g total, 3g net, here is the subtraction; and "yes, erythritol and sucralose, here is how much and why". The thread has run since June with no answer in-feed. Pin the one-time-purchase comment on every live ad.
  6. Warehouse comment-reply, one session at a time. When the warehouse has a slot, pack three real orders in one go, three cuts, no script. Until then, recut the two packing shoots we already have with new openers. It held the top add-to-cart rates in every month it ran.

7. The $115M lens: what customers are telling us, and where it cashes

Paid social is 14% of Shameless revenue over June to August and close to 100% of the listening. It ran 450 creatives over $400 in thirteen weeks, each one a message test, and collected roughly 8,000 comments a week. That is the research engine for the other 86%. The question is not whether Meta creative pays back on order one (it does not, and it is not meant to). The question is which customer signals it surfaces and which channel each one cashes in.

Three things the mix says.

Marketplace and retail are 62% of revenue and make the money. The first-order Meta loss is funded by subscription rebills ($920,349 profit in three months against -$938,559 on paid DTC). So the box that converts on Meta matters because it is the subscription on-ramp, and the trust problems that show up in Meta comments (sweetener, subscription trap, scam accusations) are Amazon-rating and retention problems wearing an ad costume.

Creative efficiency alone does not get to $115M. Moving the whole Meta book from 0.87 to the Target lane's 1.04 is worth about $91,290 a month. The same insight applied to the Amazon gallery, the pack front and the cart touches $5.1M a month.

Growth to $9.6M a month is a new-customer volume problem on Amazon and retail plus a retention problem on DTC. Both are message problems first, and the messages have been tested for three months.

What this changes about how we work. The weekly comment digest and this signal table go to the Amazon, retail and CRM owners, not just the media buyer. The messages that win on Meta are the messages to test next on the pack, the A+ page and the shelf talker. And Meta creative gets judged on what it feeds (sub take rate, star rating, retail lift), not on first-order ROAS alone.
